name: libdeflate
workload: Silesia tar single-thread in-memory deflate compression and decompression through lzbench.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4: libdeflate 1.26 -6 compresses at 82.1 MB/s, decompresses at 820 MB/s, ratio 31.85; zlib 1.3.2 -6 does 26.8 MB/s, 314 MB/s, ratio 32.19 (3.1x and 2.6x, derived from page data). -9: 30.6 MB/s and 805 MB/s versus zlib -9 11.3 MB/s and 318 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
stars_or_usage: vcpkg port libdeflate; bundled in lzbench 2.4 as v1.26 (2026-08-22)
caveats: Already catalogued; this is extra third-party evidence from the lzbench 2.4 table.
found_via: vcpkg port list and lzbench README results table

name: zlib-ng
workload: Silesia tar single-thread in-memory compression and decompression through lzbench.

name: Zstandard
workload: Silesia tar single-thread in-memory compression and decompression through lzbench.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4: zstd 1.5.7 -11 compresses at 36.1 MB/s, decompresses at 1320 MB/s, ratio 27.35; xz 5.8.4 -1 does 19.2 MB/s and 105 MB/s, ratio 27.75 (1.9x faster compression, 12.6x faster decompression and a smaller output, derived from page data). Versus zlib 1.3.2 -1 (89.0 MB/s, 297 MB/s, ratio 36.45): zstd -1 does 411 MB/s and 1351 MB/s, ratio 34.53 (4.6x and 4.5x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary); lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; compile flags not stated on the page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes)
tradeoffs: Highest levels are slow to compress.
caveats: Already catalogued; extra third-party evidence. Zstd is itself a named baseline; the wins recorded are against xz and zlib. Levels were picked from the table.

name: libdeflate
workload: In-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar, lzbench 2.4 and TurboBench nightly CI on linux-x86_64.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 on EPYC 9555P: libdeflate 1.26 -6 82.1 MB/s compress, 820 MB/s decompress, 31.85% versus zlib 1.3.2 -6 at 26.8 MB/s, 314 MB/s, 32.19%; -1: 202 MB/s and 783 MB/s at 34.68% versus zlib -1 89.0 MB/s and 297 MB/s at 36.45%; -12: 4.73 MB/s at 30.52% beating zlib -9 (11.3 MB/s, 31.92%) on ratio. TurboBench x86_64 (EPYC 7763): libdeflate 6 88.06 MB/s and 838.39 MB/s versus zlib 6 26.76 MB/s and 352.81 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4, silesia.tar; per-codec compile flags are in the lzbench Makefile, not on the results page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; TurboBench CI run on AMD EPYC 7763
tradeoffs: Whole-buffer API only, no streaming; extra memory for hash tables.
caveats: Independent re-measurement for an already catalogued project. Compression level 12 is slower than zlib -9 on speed.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): lzbench README 2.4 and TurboBench benchmark.md

name: zlib-ng
workload: In-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar, lzbench 2.4 and TurboBench nightly CI on linux-x86_64.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 on EPYC 9555P: zlib-ng 2.3.3 -6 62.1 MB/s compress, 498 MB/s decompress, 32.51% versus zlib 1.3.2 -6 at 26.8 MB/s, 314 MB/s, 32.19%; -9 25.4 MB/s and 506 MB/s versus zlib -9 11.3 MB/s and 318 MB/s at near-equal ratio. TurboBench x86_64 (EPYC 7763): zlib-ng 6 78.56 MB/s and 776.48 MB/s versus zlib 6 26.76 MB/s and 352.81 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4, silesia.tar; per-codec compile flags are in the lzbench Makefile, not on the results page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; TurboBench CI run on AMD EPYC 7763
tradeoffs: Zlib-compatible API with dual linking; level 1 output is larger than zlib -1 (44.41% versus 36.45%).
caveats: Independent re-measurement for an already catalogued project. At level 1 zlib-ng trades ratio for speed, so the like-for-like comparison is levels 6 and 9. libdeflate is faster still.

name: ISA-L (igzip)
workload: In-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar, TurboBench nightly CI on linux-x86_64.
claimed_speedup: TurboBench x86_64 (AMD EPYC 7763): igzip 1 449.15 MB/s compress, 728.71 MB/s decompress, 36.85% versus zlib 1 at 93.18 MB/s, 331.20 MB/s, 36.45%: about 4.8x faster compression at near-equal ratio (derived from page data); igzip 3 195.58 MB/s at 35.45% versus zlib 1.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub Actions runner, per TurboBench page header)
tradeoffs: x86/aarch64/RISC-V assembly-heavy storage library; igzip levels 0-3 only, output slightly larger than zlib at the same speed class.
caveats: Independent re-measurement for an already catalogued project. TurboBench CI page states no compiler or flags and the aarch64 run on an unnamed CPU shows igzip decompression slower than zlib-ng.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): TurboBench benchmark.md (linux-x86_64 table)

name: xcdat (evidence from string-index-benchmarks)
baseline: MARISA (marisa-trie 0.2.6), also CoCo-trie, PDT, FST and C2 variants
workload: Exact-match lookup in compressed string dictionaries over 13 corpora at 1M keys, 6 corpora at 10M keys, single-key lookup latency in ns.
claimed_speedup: XCDAT 15 is the fastest other structure for exact lookup on every corpus at 1M keys (words 78 ns, dna 277 ns, domains 147 ns, titles-en 243 ns, urls 365 ns, uuid 339 ns); on words the README quotes MARISA rho=2 at 346 ns against XCDAT 15 at 78 ns (about 4.4x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: c++ -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -std=c++17, GCC 16.2.1, XCDAT pinned at commit 2451441
tradeoffs: XCDAT 15 is larger than MARISA or front-coded structures (words 7.30 B/key against MARISA rho=2's 2.98). Double-array trie, static dictionary only.
caveats: Independent third-party harness, but the harness author competes with their own library (lexindex). Tier A relies on public harness, stated compiler flags and CPU. Evidence for an already catalogued project; only the MARISA comparison row is used here.

name: pasta::bit_vector (evidence from bit_vector_experiments)
baseline: CS-Poppy; experiments repo also builds sdsl-lite, sux, splatlab rankselect and rankselect2 as competitors
workload: Rank and select queries on plain bit vectors; space overhead of the rank/select index.
claimed_speedup: pasta-flat has 3.51 percent space overhead; the SIMD flat variant answers rank up to 8 percent and select up to 16.5 percent faster than CS-Poppy (README summary and search snippet of the SPIRE 2022 paper).
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 licence limits reuse; C++20 header-only; AVX2 versions for best speed.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. Reproduction code is public at https://github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments (submodules sux, sdsl-lite, rankselect, rankselect2, tlx), but I could not see results, CPU or flags (paper at arXiv 2206.01149 blocked). Gains over SDSL are not quoted on the pages I opened; the quoted percentages are against CS-Poppy.
